entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen18597" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18600" type="x-p"/> The psalmist complains to God of the oppressions which the poor suffer from the wicked man, whom he describes as the hater of the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>; proud, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>; one who will not seek God, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>; and is regardless of his judgments, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference>; self-confident, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.6">Psa 10:6</reference>; blasphemous and deceitful, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>; strives by subtlety and treachery to destroy the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.8-Psa.10.10">Psa 10:8-10</reference>; and supposes that God is regardless of his conduct, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>. The psalmist calls earnestly on God to preserve the poor and humble, and cast down the oppressor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.12-Psa.10.15">Psa 10:12-15</reference>. He foresees that his prayer is heard; that judgment will be executed, and the poor delivered, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.16-Psa.10.18">Psa 10:16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen18600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18601" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18602" type="x-p"/> Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? - This Psalm makes a part of the preceding in the Vulgate and Septuagint; and in four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. It seems to belong to the time of the captivity, or the return of the captives. It was probably made in reference to Sanballat, and the other enemies or the Jews. There is a great similarity between this and <reference osisRef="Psa.13.1-Psa.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, 35, and <reference osisRef="Psa.53.1-Psa.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference> : In these, as Calmet remarks, we find the same complaints, the same sentiments, and almost the same expressions. <div eID="gen18602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18603" type="x-p"/> God is represented here as standing at some distance, beholding the oppression of his people, and yet apparently disregarding it.
entries.content_plain: Introduction The psalmist complains to God of the oppressions which the poor suffer from the wicked man, whom he describes as the hater of the poor, Psa 10:1 , Psa 10:2 ; proud, Psa 10:3 ; one who will not seek God, Psa 10:4 ; and is regardless of his judgments, Psa 10:5 ; self-confident, Psa 10:6 ; blasphemous and deceitful, Psa 10:7 ; strives by subtlety and treachery to destroy the poor, Psa 10:8-10 ; and supposes that God is regardless of his conduct, Psa 10:11 . The psalmist calls earnestly on God to preserve the poor and humble, and cast down the oppressor, Psa 10:12-15 . He foresees that his prayer is heard; that judgment will be executed, and the poor delivered, Psa 10:16-18 . Verse 1 Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? - This Psalm makes a part of the preceding in the Vulgate and Septuagint; and in four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. It seems to belong to the time of the captivity, or the return of the captives. It was probably made in reference to Sanballat, and the other enemies or the Jews. There is a great similarity between this and Psa 13:1-6 , Psa 14:1-7 , 35, and Psa 53:1-6 : In these, as Calmet remarks, we find the same complaints, the same sentiments, and almost the same expressions. God is represented here as standing at some distance, beholding the oppression of his people, and yet apparently disregarding it.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18604" type="x-p"/> The wicked in his pride - On no principle of nature or reason can we account for a wicked man persecuting a humble follower of God because of his religion. The devil hates godliness; and the wicked man hates it also because the devil is in his heart.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> Boasteth of his heart's desire - Boasts among his fellows how often he has gratified such and such passions, in such and such circumstances. This shows the excess of a depraved and imbruted spirit. He who can boast of his iniquity, is in the broad road to perdition. Should such a one repent and turn to God, it would be equal to any miracle. <div eID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18606" type="x-p"/> Blesseth the covetous, whom the Lord abhorreth - Or, he blesseth the covetous, he abhorreth the Lord. Those who are like himself he commends, and with them he associates; and they abhor the Lord - they have a mortal hatred against every thing that is holy; and they are under the full influence of that carnal mind which is enmity to the Lord.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> His ways are always grievous - Or, He is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times. He is full of lust, or irregular and unholy desires; he conceives and brings forth sin; and sin being finished, time, place, and opportunity concurring, death is soon brought forth. <div eID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> Thy judgments are far above out of his sight - He is so blinded with sin, that he cannot see the operations of God's hand. <div eID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18610" type="x-p"/> He puffeth at them - He whistles at them; insults God, and despises men. He overthrows them with his breath; he has only to give orders, and they are destroyed. "Bring me the head of Giaffer," said an Asiatic despot. The head was immediately brought! No trial, no judge, no jury; but the despot's will and caprice.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18613" type="x-p"/> He sitteth in the lurking places - In this and the following verse there appears to be an allusion to espionage, or setting of spies on a man's conduct; or to the conduct of an assassin or private murderer. He sitteth in lurking places - in secret places; his eyes - spies - are privily set; he lieth in wait secretly: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net. He is like a hunter that lays his traps and gins, digs his pits, sets his nets; and when the prey falls into them, he destroys its life.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen18630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18631" type="x-p"/> That the man of the earth may no more oppress - I believe the Hebrew will be better translated thus: "That he may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land." Destroy the influence of the tyrant; and let him not have it again in his power to add even one additional act of oppression to those which he has already committed. <div eID="gen18631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18632" type="x-p"/> How many for the sake of their religion, and because they would serve God with a pure conscience, have, by wicked lords, proud and arrogant land owners, been driven off their farms, turned out of their houses, deprived of their employments, and exposed to wretchedness! While they served the devil, and were regardless of their souls, they had quiet and peaceable possession; but when they turned to the Lord, and became sober and industrious, attended the means of grace, read their Bible, and were frequent in prayer, then the vile man of the earth drove them from their dwellings! In the sight of such Philistines, piety towards God is the highest of crimes. What a dreadful account must these give to the Judge of the Fatherless and the oppressed!  <chapter eID="Ps.10"/> <div eID="gen18632" type="x-p"/>
